title: Different hands, same prayer
hook: schools differ on hand placement and small details, and all are valid within the tradition

segments.voice: Yesterday: rak'ah, one full unit of prayer, seventeen a day. Your line was two, four, four, three, four. Did it stick by tonight? Day one hundred ten.

Stand at the back of a big mosque during Friday prayer and look down the line. The man on the left has his hands folded low, below the navel. The one next to him, higher, on the chest. The one next to him has his arms hanging straight at his sides. At the end of the Fatiha, some say amin out loud; some whisper it. A newcomer might think half the room is doing it wrong. Nobody in the line thinks so. They're shoulder to shoulder, and they bow at the same moment. Today: different hands, same prayer.
screen: `HANDS LOW, HANDS HIGH, ARMS DOWN.` → `AMIN ALOUD, AMIN WHISPERED.` → `THEY BOW AT THE SAME MOMENT.`

segments.voice: The word is madhhab, a school of law. Literally it means a way of going, the road someone takes. In the first centuries of Islam, scholars in different cities worked out how to follow the Qur'an and the Prophet's ﷺ example in daily life, and the ones whose methods lasted became schools. Among Sunni Muslims there are four, each named after a scholar: Abu Hanifa in Iraq, Malik in Medina, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school, named after Ja'far al-Sadiq. Why do they differ on something as simple as hands? Because the reports differ. Companions saw the Prophet pray over years, in different places, and remembered different details. So the Hanafi school commonly teaches hands folded below the navel; the Shafi'i, above the navel, below the chest; the Maliki school is known for leaving the arms at the sides, and so is Ja'fari practice. Each has its reasons, going back to a report. There's a well-known story about Imam Malik. A caliph, the story goes, wanted to make Malik's book, the Muwatta, the law for the whole empire. Malik said no. The companions, he said, had spread out to different lands, and each land had its own knowledge from them. Leave people with what they have. People sometimes quote a saying, the differing of my community is a mercy. Scholars note it isn't a reliable hadith. But the attitude holds: within the tradition, all four Sunni schools are considered valid, and a Muslim can pray behind someone of another school. The details differ. The prayer is one.
screen: `MADHHAB — A WAY OF GOING.` · `FOUR SUNNI SCHOOLS, AND THE JA'FARI.` · `THE REPORTS DIFFER.` · `MALIK SAID: LEAVE PEOPLE BE.` · then, large: `THE DETAILS DIFFER. THE PRAYER IS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch two people pray differently, calmly. If you can, find a short video of a prayer, or picture the line in that mosque. Look at the hands. Low, high, at the sides. Notice if anything in you wants to decide who's right. Let that go. Then stand, and try each yourself for one breath: hands low, hands high, arms hanging. Notice the prayer doesn't change. If you pray, you already know your own way; just hold it gently. The bell holds the time.
Madhhab. A school of Islamic law, a way of going; four Sunni schools and the Ja'fari, one prayer. Today's word.
Your line: many hands, one prayer. Today, when someone does a familiar thing a little differently from you, notice what's the same underneath. Day one hundred ten.

howItsDone: A Muslim usually prays according to one school of law, often the one of their family or region, and pray side by side in the mosque with people who hold their hands, say amin or raise their hands a little differently.

original.note: Arabic: a school of law; literally, a way of going, a road taken.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims who pray differently belong to different sects.
what it means: a madhhab is a school of law; the four Sunni schools differ on details and count each other valid.
what a scholar hears: ikhtilaf, legitimate disagreement from differing reports, and the story of Malik declining to impose the Muwatta.

sources.ref: The report of Imam Malik declining to have the Muwatta imposed (in biographical works on Malik, e.g. Ibn Sa'd and later compilers)
Sahih al-Bukhari 740 (placing the right hand on the left in prayer, from Sahl ibn Sa'd)

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: 'most Shia follow the Ja'fari school' made precise (Twelver Shia) in teach and match; 'many Malikis and Ja'faris' replaced with the schools' known positions; 'the attitude runs deep' stock line cut; howItsDone no longer claims 'most Muslims'.
The Malik–caliph story exists in several versions (al-Mansur or Harun al-Rashid); sourcing is from biographical literature, not hadith. Please confirm the best reference.

Hand positions stated as common teachings: Hanafi below the navel (men), Shafi'i above the navel below the chest, many Malikis at the sides (sadl), Ja'fari at the sides; Hanbali positions vary and are not stated. Please check.
Amin aloud (Shafi'i, Hanbali) vs. silently (Hanafi, Maliki) described without naming schools.
'The differing of my community is a mercy' is widely judged to have no reliable chain; stated as such.
Whether Sunni and Shia pray behind each other is a separate, more sensitive question; the script only claims mutual validity among the four Sunni schools.
